corrected_value.title_o: Social inequality and the reduction of ideological dissonance on behalf of the system: evidence of enhanced system justification among the disadvantaged
corrected_value.title: Social inequality and the reduction of ideological dissonance on behalf of the system: evidence of enhanced system justification among the disadvantaged

decisions.quote:
System justification theory (SJT) posits that members of low-status groups are more likely to see their
                                social systems as legitimate than members of high-status groups because members of low-status groups
                                experience a sense of dissonance between system motivations and self/group motivations (Jost, Pelham,
                                Sheldon, & Sullivan, 2003). The author examined the status–legitimacy hypothesis using data from 3
                                representative sets of data from the United States (American National Election Studies and General
                                Social Surveys) and throughout the world (World Values Survey; total N across studies ⫽ 151,794).
decisions.reason: Brandt (2013) explicitly re-tests the status–legitimacy hypothesis originally reported by Jost, Pelham, Sheldon, and Sullivan (2003; published online in 2002, DOI 10.1002/ejsp.127), which found enhanced system justification/legitimacy among low-status groups in U.S. national surveys. Both the shipped record and blind target 0 identify this same original paper (10.1002/ejsp.127).

decisions.quote:
Multilevel models revealed that the average effect across years in the United States and countries
                                throughout the world was most often directly contrary to the status–legitimacy hypothesis or was
                                practically zero. In short, the status–legitimacy effect is not a robust phenomenon. Two theoretically
                                relevant moderator variables (inequality and civil liberties) were also tested, revealing weak evidence,
                                null evidence, or contrary evidence to the dissonance-inspired status–legitimacy hypothesis. In sum, the
                                status–legitimacy effect is not robust and is unlikely to be the result of dissonance.
decisions.reason: For the resolved original study Jost et al. (2003, 10.1002/ejsp.127) and replication record type, the author states an explicit overall verdict (and titles a Discussion subsection 'Failure to Replicate') concluding that the average effect across U.S. years and countries worldwide was most often directly contrary to the status–legitimacy hypothesis or practically zero (with zero of 10 U.S. main effects supporting the hypothesis and only 1 of 14 overall), so the status–legitimacy effect is not robust. Under Step 3 Rule 1 of the codebook, the author's overall verdict governs over single isolated estimates and establishes the replication outcome as 'failed'.

decisions.reason: Brandt (2013) re-tests the published status–legitimacy finding of Jost et al. (2003, 10.1002/ejsp.127) using expanded representative survey samples spanning 31 U.S. survey years (ANES 1958–2008 and GSS 1975–2010, adding 26 more U.S. survey years beyond those in Jost et al.) and 65 countries in the World Values Survey (total N = 151,794), while mentioning a reanalysis of shared years only as an unprinted footnote check. Because the study uses a different, expanded sample to re-test a previously published finding, both shipped and blind codings correctly classify the type as 'replication'.
